question: Which ATT&CK techniques do CAPEC-13, CAPEC-640 map to (they overlap), and what mitigations apply to the deduplicated union?

answer.headline: Gathered 9 record(s) from 2 source(s); 2 question(s) the sources don't establish.
answer.narrative: CAPEC-13 (Subverting Environment Variable Values) and CAPEC-640 (Inclusion of Code in Existing Process) both have a Status of Stable and an Abstraction of Detailed. CAPEC-13 has 4 mitigations (capec:attack-pattern:13:mitigation:4, capec:attack-pattern:13:mitigation:1, capec:attack-pattern:13:mitigation:2, capec:attack-pattern:13:mitigation:3), 1 CanPrecede successor (CAPEC-14), and 1 ChildOf parent (CAPEC-77). CAPEC-640 has 7 mitigations (capec:attack-pattern:640:mitigation:7, capec:attack-pattern:640:mitigation:1, capec:attack-pattern:640:mitigation:2, capec:attack-pattern:640:mitigation:3, capec:attack-pattern:640:mitigation:4, capec:attack-pattern:640:mitigation:5, capec:attack-pattern:640:mitigation:6). The attack source doesn't establish the mapped ATT&CK techniques or their mitigations because the sub-question it depends on (q6) produced no seed identifiers.

records.name: Inclusion of Code in Existing Process
records.label: AttackPattern
records.description: The adversary takes advantage of a bug in an application failing to verify the integrity of the running process to execute arbitrary code in the address space of a separate live process. The adversary could use running code in the context of another process to try to access process's memory, system/network resources, etc. The goal of this attack is to evade detection defenses and escalate privileges by masking the malicious code under an existing legitimate process. Examples of approaches include but not limited to: dynamic-link library (DLL) injection, portable executable injection, thread execution hijacking, ptrace system calls, VDSO hijacking, function hooking, reflective code loading, and more.

related.name: Manipulating User-Controlled Variables
related.label: AttackPattern
related.description: This attack targets user controlled variables (DEBUG=1, PHP Globals, and So Forth). An adversary can override variables leveraging user-supplied, untrusted query variables directly used on the application server without any data sanitization. In extreme cases, the adversary can change variables controlling the business logic of the application. For instance, in languages like PHP, a number of poorly set default configurations may allow the user to override variables.
